newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Dial-a-prime minister service opens in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Dial-a-prime minister service opens in Pakistan.

text.p: Dial a special Islamabad telephone number and talk to Pakistan's new prime minister. "This is Nawaz Sharif speaking. Who is calling?" he says.
Sharif, who won a landslide election victory on February 3, has told Pakistanis he will answer their telephone calls in person for half an hour every morning for 10 days.
He is seeking their advice on how to set up local watchdog committees across the country to monitor government and police activities, but many callers have other things on their minds.
The lucky ones who got through on Thursday had suggestions on anything from kite-flying to birth control.
"Please close the snooker clubs in Islamabad by 10 p.m.," one anxious citizen told Sharif. "They are open all night and a lot of money is gambled. They should be just for entertainment.
"Secondly, there is no concept of family planning in Islam so this programme should be closed. Money is being wasted on that, while children are born sick and handicapped," he said.
The man talked through the 60 seconds allotted to each call and was cut off before the prime minister could reply.
Thousands of people have tried to call Sharif's number since he opened the hotline on Tuesday, jamming the exchange.
"We had 300,000 calls on Wednesday," Sharif's press adviser Siddiqul Farooq told Reuters. "Some don't make a suggestion or demand anything, they are just excited to talk to him."
He said Sharif was issuing immediate instructions after hearing complaints and proposals. "Some people are amazed at the speed at which the administration responds," Farooq said.
Sharif told one caller seeking financial help for a paralysed daughter to provide her address. "Someone will get in touch with you very soon," he assured the distressed woman.
Another caller suggested that a hotline to the government should be permanently available for citizens' complaints.
One woman urged Sharif to ban Basant, a popular kite-flying festival due to take place in Islamabad on Friday. "We want to stop Basant," she said.
"In Lahore, a lot of money was spent on Basant, but you should stop it in Islamabad."
Sharif, who comes from Lahore, chuckled.
